name: Heavy Metal
about: Heavy metal came out of Birmingham in 1970, when Black Sabbath slowed the blues rock of Cream and Led Zeppelin, tuned down and sang about doom, and the family that grew from it is defined by distorted, riff-driven guitar, heavy drums and a voice that either soars or snarls. Judas Priest codified the twin-guitar sound, the New Wave of British Heavy Metal produced Iron Maiden and Motörhead, and in the 1980s the music split: thrash in California with Metallica and Slayer, glam on the Sunset Strip, and the extreme branches, death, black, doom and grindcore, in Florida, Norway and Sweden. The 1990s brought Pantera's groove and nu metal, the 2000s metalcore, Mastodon and a progressive turn. It is now a global music with hundreds of substyles and an audience that never left.

artists.name: Metallica
artists.why: took thrash to the world's stadiums

artists.name: Slayer
artists.why: thrash at its fastest and darkest

albums.title: Paranoid
albums.why: War Pigs, Iron Man and the title track in one sitting: the record that turned heavy blues into a genre, and still the one every metal shelf begins with.

albums.title: Sad Wings of Destiny
albums.why: Victim of Changes and Tyrant brought operatic vocals, twin leads and gothic drama to the blueprint, the first album that sounds like metal as later understood.

albums.title: Ace of Spades
albums.why: Lemmy's band at full velocity, the point where punk speed and metal weight became one thing and thrash became possible.

albums.title: The Number of the Beast
albums.why: Bruce Dickinson's first album with Maiden made the NWOBHM's galloping bass and twin harmonies a worldwide language, with Hallowed Be Thy Name as its epic.

albums.title: Black Metal
albums.why: Sloppy, cartoonish and recorded badly, but its Satanic imagery and sheer nastiness named black metal and lit the fuse for every extreme style.

albums.title: Holy Diver
albums.why: Ronnie James Dio's solo debut, with Vivian Campbell's guitar and Rainbow in Dark, is the classic-metal vocal record against which the rest are measured.

albums.title: Don't Break the Oath
albums.why: King Diamond's falsetto and Hank Shermann's winding riffs on the Danish band's occult classic, a key source for both thrash and black metal.

albums.title: Master of Puppets
albums.why: Thrash at its most composed and ambitious, with Cliff Burton's last recordings and the title track's eight minutes, the consensus greatest metal album of the 1980s.

albums.title: Reign in Blood
albums.why: Twenty-nine minutes, ten songs, produced by Rick Rubin to a diamond edge; the fastest, most brutal record of its decade and never bettered on its own terms.

albums.title: Epicus Doomicus Metallicus
albums.why: Leif Edling's Swedish band took Sabbath's slowest moments, added operatic vocals and funereal grandeur, and named the genre of epic doom in the process.

albums.title: Among the Living
albums.why: New York's thrash contingent at their tightest, with Caught in a Mosh and I Am the Law, and a sense of humour the Bay Area bands lacked.

albums.title: Scream Bloody Gore
albums.why: Chuck Schuldiner's debut is generally called the first death metal album: crude, horror-obsessed and the beginning of a whole extreme-metal lineage.

albums.title: Scum
albums.why: Two different line-ups, one-second songs and a political fury that invented grindcore; Birmingham's second great contribution to heavy music.

albums.title: Keeper of the Seven Keys Part I
albums.why: Michael Kiske's arrival turned Helloween's speed metal into soaring, melodic power metal, the German template that Europe followed for two decades.

albums.title: Rust in Peace
albums.why: Dave Mustaine's definitive line-up, with Marty Friedman on lead, delivers thrash's most technically accomplished record in Holy Wars and Hangar 18.

albums.title: Vulgar Display of Power
albums.why: Dimebag Darrell's grooves and Phil Anselmo's bark set the sound of 1990s American metal, loud enough to survive grunge and nu metal both.

albums.title: Sleep's Holy Mountain
albums.why: Three Californians worshipping at the altar of Sabbath and marijuana, the record that gave stoner metal its name, pace and sense of humour.

albums.title: Chaos A.D.
albums.why: The Brazilian band slowed their thrash into groove and tribal percussion, and in Refuse/Resist made the sound of the global South heard in metal.

albums.title: Bloody Kisses
albums.why: Peter Steele's Brooklyn gothic-doom band at their most seductive, with Black No. 1 and Christian Woman, the gothic metal record that crossed over.

albums.title: De Mysteriis Dom Sathanas
albums.why: Recorded amid murder and church burnings, with Attila Csihar's chanted vocals and Euronymous's icy riffs, the founding album of Norwegian black metal.

albums.title: Toxicity
albums.why: Armenian-American nu metal with Rick Rubin production, political bite and Serj Tankian's manic range; the best-made record of its much-maligned style.

albums.title: Leviathan
albums.why: Moby-Dick retold as sludge-prog, with Brann Dailor's drumming and Blood and Thunder, the record that announced metal's 2000s generation.

albums.title: From Mars to Sirius
albums.why: The French quartet's breakthrough combines death-metal precision, environmental grief and a whale-song sense of scale that modern metal has imitated since.

albums.title: Pleasure to Kill
albums.why: German thrash at its rawest and most relentless, a record that made Essen a thrash capital and that death metal's founders studied closely.

albums.title: Nightmare Logic
albums.why: Dallas crossover thrash with hardcore energy and Riley Gale's bark, the most widely loved metal album of the late 2010s and a bridge to a new audience.

albums.title: Hidden History of the Human Race
albums.why: Denver's cosmic death metal ends with an eighteen-minute epic, a record that brought old-school death metal to listeners well outside the scene.
